note.title: Rate of photosynthesis and Required Practical 6
note.overview: The rate of photosynthesis can be limited by light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature or chlorophyll amount. You must interpret limiting-factor graphs, calculate rate and plan Required Practical 6 using pondweed to investigate the effect of light intensity.
learningGoals: Explain how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and chlorophyll amount affect photosynthesis rate.
Interpret rate graphs, identify the limiting factor and explain why a graph plateaus or falls.
Plan and evaluate Required Practical 6, calculate rate and identify variables and controls.

temperature → a factor affecting the enzyme-controlled reactions of photosynthesis
chlorophyll amount → a factor that can limit how much light energy a plant absorbs

commonMistakes: Do not assume light is always the limiting factor; a plateau means another factor is restricting the rate.
Do not say high temperature always increases photosynthesis; above the optimum, enzyme function is disrupted and rate falls.
Rate needs a time component, for example oxygen volume per minute.
Keep temperature controlled when moving a lamp because lamps can also heat the water.
Bubble count can be less reliable than gas volume because bubble size varies.
detailedExplanation: This topic is verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Biology Curriculum Outline 2026–27, which includes rate of photosynthesis in Spring 2 and specifically requires Practical 6 on the effect of light intensity using an aquatic organism such as pondweed.

When light is limiting, increasing light intensity increases the rate because more light energy is available. Once another factor becomes limiting, increasing light further produces little or no increase, so the graph reaches a plateau.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate while carbon dioxide is limiting. Again, the rate eventually plateaus when another factor limits photosynthesis.

Temperature affects enzyme-controlled reactions. At low temperatures the rate is slower. Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum; at temperatures that are too high, enzymes lose their functional shape and the rate falls. Low chlorophyll amount can also reduce the rate because less light energy is absorbed.

For Required Practical 6, vary light intensity by changing lamp distance or measuring light intensity. Measure oxygen production over a fixed time; measuring gas volume is more reliable than simply counting bubbles because bubbles can differ in size. Keep temperature, carbon dioxide availability, pondweed species/length and measurement time constant.

Repeat each light condition and calculate a mean. Calculate rate as oxygen volume ÷ time, then plot rate against light intensity (or the specified distance measure). When explaining the graph, identify which factor is limiting in each region rather than merely describing the line.
examTips: For a graph question, describe the pattern and then explain the limiting factor causing each region.
For practical design, name IV, DV, key controls, repeats/mean and the graph you would plot.
Use rate = amount of oxygen produced ÷ time and always include units.
If a graph plateaus, state that the tested factor is no longer limiting and another factor is now in shortest supply.
